title: Build the controlling focus
summary: Write one clear central response, give every paragraph a distinct job within it and remove or repair details that do not advance it.

sections.title: One plan needs one centre
content: E6.3 selected and ordered two connected applications of one school-learned method. A controlling focus now states the central response that those applications will prove. It is more precise than a topic and broader than one event detail.

Topic: breaking a large task into smaller parts. Controlling focus: this method is useful beyond mathematics because it turns a complicated event into manageable decisions and helps the writer adapt when plans change.

sections.title: Build a three-part focus statement
content: A strong controlling focus names the school learning, its different area of application and the main insight the composition will demonstrate. For an explanatory task, the insight should answer how or why the transfer matters rather than announce only that it is useful.

Use this frame when needed: ‘The school-learned [method or idea] helps in [different area] because [specific effect or insight].’ Treat the frame as a thinking tool; vary the wording in the final composition.

sections.title: Give each paragraph a job
content: Controlling focus: breaking a large task into smaller parts made the charity sale manageable and helped the writer respond calmly when conditions changed.

Paragraph job one: show how dividing publicity, supplies, prices and staffing created a workable plan before the event. Paragraph job two: show how the same method identified urgent tasks and guided reassignment when rain moved the stalls indoors. Closing insight: the method reduces confusion because the writer can act on one clear part at a time.
The paragraphs do different work, but both advance the same claim. A new paragraph about teamwork as a separate school lesson would start a second centre and weaken control.

sections.title: Run the link-back check
content: After every planned paragraph, complete this sentence privately: ‘This advances my focus because…’. A strong answer names the relationship between the paragraph's evidence and the central response. If the answer merely says ‘it is related’, the paragraph's job is still unclear.
For the rain paragraph: ‘This advances my focus because reprioritising the separate tasks shows how the same method supports calm adaptation when the original plan changes.’

sections.title: Use thread words without copying
content: Repeat the central meaning across the plan with controlled variation. ‘Breaking the task into parts’, ‘the step-by-step method’ and ‘working through one priority at a time’ can maintain the thread without copying the same sentence.

Topic sentences should name each paragraph's new contribution as well as the shared thread. A topic sentence that only repeats the controlling focus does not tell the reader what new work the paragraph will do.

sections.title: Repair focus failures
content: A vague focus names a topic but no central response. A split focus tries to prove two unrelated main ideas. Detail drift supplies interesting information whose connection cannot be explained. An overclaim promises more than the evidence can show, such as saying one method always guarantees success.

Repair a vague focus by adding the application and insight. Repair a split focus by choosing one centre. Repair drift by linking, reframing or removing the detail. Repair an overclaim by matching the strength of the statement to the available evidence.

sections.title: Make every paragraph advance the response
content: Use the E6.3 idea chain to make six focus decisions. Complete the group before viewing feedback, then carry the focus statement and paragraph jobs into the five-minute plan in E6.5.
